prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened a new regime of precision at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight round-1 statements I find that nothing in them weakens the scientific case, and the chair's first question is one I think the committee can answer in the citation. The 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb as a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single trapped quantum systems, in practice ions. The lattice clock rests on a different physical idea: a state-insensitive (magic-wavelength) trap makes a large ensemble of neutral atoms an oscillator limited by quantum projection noise, with Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors removed by design. That is why the result is a new regime and not a better ruler. As a theorist who lives close to the superconducting-circuit and many-body community, what convinces me is that the clock now shows physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants, ultralight dark-matter searches and many-body interaction effects inside the sample. It is also reproduced and compared across several laboratories, which is the robustness test I care most about. Attribution is as clean as a metrology field allows: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first realisation, and Ye's group took the strontium clock to the accuracy frontier.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real and I do not want to hide them. First, a minority can still read this as the third metrology prize in twenty years and as an instrument achievement. I think the citation answers that, but it is a judgement and not something the record settles. Second, two names will leave out Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, the JILA collaborators and the ion-clock groups. Like most colleagues, I am recalling priority from memory, and I would want the first lattice-clock papers examined before the vote, with the citation worded so that it says lattice clocks and does not claim all optical clocks. Third, the SI second has not been redefined. I treat the planned redefinition as evidence of community acceptance, so this is mainly a timing argument and not a scientific objection, but I accept Kroll's point that a prize slightly before the redefinition is a choice the committee should make knowingly. Against B001, which I still rank third: the pairing mechanism is open, and the three-name limit omits Cao, the other first experimentalists and earlier twisted-bilayer theory. Against my own opening choice B058: I cannot judge it impartially, the 2025 prize is very close in subject, and Wallraff is outside the trio.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the 2025 prize already covers the superconducting-circuit platform and that B058 is partly a technology claim with the Wallraff gap unresolved. He keeps B007 as his preferred part and names B001 and B039 as fallbacks.
responses.response: I accept this argument and have stopped defending B058, and I have no wish to reopen it in this round. I also agree with his answer to the 'invention or discovery' objection, that the discovery is the demonstrated ability to cancel systematic shifts for thousands of atoms at once and what that opens up. I would add that the test is whether the instrument produces results about nature, and the lattice clock does so in a way the comb and the ion clock did not. Where I would go a little further than he does is on the secretary's point that the redefinition is a measure of maturity. I would keep it out of the citation, because the prize should reward the physics and not a standards decision that is still pending.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B001 for a continuum-model prediction followed by an experiment at exactly the predicted angle, and calls the lattice clock further along in maturity and cleaner in attribution than B001 even though he ranked it fifth. He keeps B023 as his second choice.
responses.response: His own comparison in case_against says the clock is the more mature and more cleanly attributed candidate, and that is the point on which I think we are closer than our first choices suggest. I share his admiration for the prediction-then-experiment loop in twisted bilayer graphene and I ranked it third. My remaining concern is the one he states, an eight-year-old field with an unresolved pairing mechanism and a contested three-name allocation. I would support a narrower B001 citation limited to flat bands at the magic angle and the observed correlated insulators and superconductivity, without any claim about the mechanism, but I do not think it should displace B007 this year. On B023 I defer to him and Mehlig on whether the 2016 prize overlaps, because that is not my field, and I note that I ranked it eighth.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B001 because the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is transparent and the essential mechanism is understood, and he says himself that if the committee finds B001 not yet settled, the lattice clock is the more mature and less contested choice.
responses.response: That sentence is the most useful bridge in the whole round-1 exchange: we agree on what the fallback is, and our difference is whether to wait. I agree that the continuum model is the kind of transparent theory a prize should reward. The clock has the same structure on another scale, a simple general condition, magic wavelength, tested to extraordinary accuracy. The part of his argument I would press on is that the mechanism is understood at the level of the essential model, because the superconductivity is still debated, and that is exactly why I think a prize is better a few years later when the phase diagram is settled. I would be glad to see B001 prized then.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which determines how the citation is worded, and she lists Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom as contributors outside the two names. She also asks that my possible conflict be handled openly.
responses.response: I agree that the wording of the citation is where this question is decided, and I would propose that it names the lattice (the trapping of many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength) and the 10^-18 regime, so that ion clocks and the comb stay clearly outside. On credit I cannot settle from memory whether any of the early lattice-clock contributors would change the allocation, so I support an expert check of the first publications before the vote. If the record shows a name that cannot be left out, I would rather say so openly than defend two names by habit. On the conflict, I have recused myself on B058 in my own note and will not argue for it, so it will not set my ranking.

responses.point: As chair, Pearce asks what the committee can settle from the record and what is judgement, and asks whether the optical lattice clock is a discovery or an instrument advance. He moved to B007 from IceCube and treats the overlap objection as real but not disqualifying.
responses.response: I would split his question in the way he suggests. From the record we can settle who proposed the magic-wavelength lattice, who first realised it, which groups first reached 10^-18, and what the first publications claim. Whether this counts as a discovery or an instrument is judgement, and I think the instrument-driven standard he applies to IceCube applies equally here: a new measurement capability with controlled systematics and independent confirmation. His own move away from B039 for credit reasons seems right to me, since splitting credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering inside a very large collaboration is harder than the two-name clock case. On the chair's question about the SI second, I regard it as a point about timing and not about maturity, because the clocks are already reproduced across laboratories.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether a prize before the redefinition of the second is timely or slightly early, and he notes that B007 leaves only two names, so it pairs naturally with no second part of the shortlist. He also discloses time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder.
responses.response: On timing I would say that the redefinition is an administrative decision that follows from the physics and does not make it. The prize does not need to wait for it, though waiting would not be unreasonable. I agree with his observation about configuration and it is why I now propose a single part. A second part would force a reduction of names that I cannot justify for B007 or B001. I do not see his time in Hall's laboratory as a conflict for B007, but it is right that he disclosed it to the chair and I would leave the recusal decision to the chair.

uncertainties: Whether the early lattice-clock record changes the credit boundary beyond Katori and Ye, and I am relying on memory of the priority history and would want the first publications checked by the experts.
Whether the committee reads the optical lattice clock as a discovery of a new measurement regime or as a third metrology prize, which is a judgement that the record will not settle.
Whether to award before or after the SI second is redefined. I consider this a timing question and not a maturity question, but I am not certain colleagues agree.

Whether twisted bilayer graphene (B001) would be a stronger choice if the pairing mechanism is resolved; I have not changed my view that waiting a few years improves it, but I am outside condensed matter and defer to Eriksson and Mehlig on the maturity of the phase diagram.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work with Chalmers superconducting-circuit groups, and Chalmers hosted 2025 laureates Martinis and Clarke as WACQT guests. I recuse myself on B058 (circuit QED), which I ranked first at opening, and I do not support it in my final configuration; my opening support for it should be discounted. Olsson and I are in the same Chalmers physics department, and I note this in connection with her round-1 disagreement. My work on giant atoms and the dynamical Casimir effect is adjacent to B058, not to B007. I have no specific connection to B007, B001 or B008 and no known connection to Katori or Ye.
